title: Closures remember their surroundings
keyIdeas: A closure = a function + references to the variables around where it was defined.
Returned inner functions keep access to the outer function's variables.
Each outer call creates fresh, independent private state.
`var` in loops shares one variable; `let`/`const` bind per iteration.

workedExample.problem: Build `makeRateLimiter(limit)` returning a function `tryRequest()` that returns `true` for the first `limit` calls and `false` afterwards. Two limiters must not affect each other.
steps: Keep the changing state — calls used so far — in a `let` inside `makeRateLimiter`; it is private to the closure.
Return an inner function that compares the count with `limit` (also captured) and increments only when allowed.
Calling `makeRateLimiter` again creates a new environment with its own counter.
workedExample.answer: `api()` returns `true, true, false`; `other` independently allows exactly one call — each closure has its own `used`.

pitfalls: Declaring the state *outside* the factory (e.g. a module-level `let used`), so every limiter shares it.
Creating callbacks in a `for (var i ...)` loop and expecting each to see a different `i`.
Returning the result of calling the inner function instead of the function itself.

citations.quote: A closure is the combination of a function bundled together (enclosed) with references to its surrounding state (the lexical environment).
In JavaScript, closures are created every time a function is created, at function creation time.
Notice how the two counters maintain their independence from one another. Each closure references a different version of the privateCounter variable
This example uses const instead of var, so every closure binds the block-scoped variable, meaning that no additional closures are required.
